items.title: What IntersectionObserver can't do
items.current:
What IntersectionObserver can't do

An IntersectionObserver measures a target against a root, and that root has to be an ancestor of the target, or the viewport. That is the whole model.

"Is this floating card mostly over that background band?" involves two elements with no ancestor relationship at all — they are siblings, or cousins, or in unrelated parts of the tree. There is no root you can pass that expresses it, and no threshold array that recovers it. The answer you want is the overlap of two arbitrary rectangles, which is a different question from the one IO was built to answer.

items.title: IntersectionObserver still does the expensive half
items.current:
IntersectionObserver still does the expensive half

Rectangle math is cheap; doing it for every element on a long page, every frame, is not. So canvas-watch keeps two IntersectionObservers whose only job is to decide what is worth measuring:

[table] Observer / Watches / Effect
Element gate — Every watched element — An element off screen is dropped from the measured set entirely. Its rect is never read and its class is cleared.
Zone gate — Every trigger zone, with a triggerRootMargin of 200px by default — Only zones near the viewport stay candidates, so a page with two hundred zones compares against the handful currently in play.

The result is that per-frame cost tracks what is on screen rather than how long the document is, and a page with nothing visible to resolve schedules no work at all. IO is doing what it is genuinely good at — cheap, off-main-thread visibility signals — and the rectangle comparison only runs on what survives that filter.

items.title: Watched element and trigger zone
items.current:
Watched element

A floating element you tag with watch-bg-canvas (or register through an adapter). It receives an over-* class describing the zone it currently sits over.

Trigger zone

A background element tagged with a *-trigger class. Each maps to an over-* class by convention: strip the -trigger suffix, add the over- prefix.

A floating element you tag with watch-bg-canvas (or register through an adapter). It receives an over-* class describing the zone it currently sits over.

Trigger zone

items.reason: The colon plus comma made the convention read like two disconnected instructions. "So you strip X and add Y" is one move, which is what it is.

items.title: Winner rule
items.current:
Winner = deepest, then majority overlap

Only zones covering at least threshold of the watched element's own area are eligible — 50% by default. Among those, the most deeply nested zone wins outright; among zones at the same depth, the largest overlap wins. If nothing clears the threshold, every over-* class is removed.

Nesting beats area because a zone inside another zone is the more specific answer — otherwise a container could never be overridden, since its overlap is by definition at least its children's. Depth only reorders zones that already clear the threshold, so a nested zone that barely clips the element can't hijack it. Same-class rectangles count by their physical union, so duplicate pixels are never counted twice, and coverage stays paired with its depth so a tiny nested zone cannot promote a same-class ancestor. The heading at the top of this page is a zone of its own inside the hero's: the bar takes dark ink while it is crossing those pale letters, and the hero's light ink everywhere else.

items.title: createCanvasWatcher description and option table
items.current:
Returns a live watcher in the browser, or a no-op during SSR — so you never need to guard typeof window. Invalid thresholds, margins, selectors and class mappings fail before any browser resources are allocated.

watchSelector — Selector for elements to watch.
triggerSelector — Coarse selector for trigger elements; refined in JS by triggerSuffix.
triggerSuffix — Suffix that marks a class as a trigger.
appliedPrefix — Prefix for the applied class.
classMap — Explicit triggerClass → appliedClass overrides; these win over the convention.
threshold — Fraction of the watched element's own area that must overlap to count.
triggerRootMargin — Margin in px around the viewport for keeping a trigger zone "active".

triggerSelector — Coarse selector for trigger elements, refined in JS by triggerSuffix.
triggerSuffix — Suffix that marks a class as a trigger.

items.title: Watcher methods, helpers and validation
items.current:
refresh() — Re-scan watch, trigger and declarative viewport elements.
watch(el) — Register one overlap owner. Returns an idempotent unwatch() function.
observeViewport(reference, listener) — Subscribe one owner to vertical viewport state. Returns an idempotent unsubscribe function.
schedule() — Force a recompute on the next frame.
destroy() — Terminally cancel work, disconnect observers and remove owned classes.

Every registration owns an independent disposer, even when an element or callback is repeated. destroy() is terminal. A consumer listener that throws is reported through reportError without blocking healthy listeners or cleanup.

Shared watcher and pure helpers

getSharedWatcher() — The realm-wide singleton the Svelte adapter uses. Join it to share one rAF loop.
refreshCanvasWatch() — Re-scan the shared watcher. Call after client-side navigation.
scheduleRefresh() — The same coalesced re-scan; refreshCanvasWatch() is a named alias for it.
overlapArea(a, b) — Intersection area of two rects, or 0. Pure.
pickWinningClass(totals, area, threshold) — The winner rule itself, depth and all. Pure.
resolveAppliedClass(triggerClass, opts) — One trigger class to its applied class, or null. Pure.
classifyViewportRect(rect, top, bottom) — A rect's vertical state against two bounds. Pure.

Validation errors

Bad configuration throws immediately rather than failing quietly on the first frame.

items.title: Per-frame walkthrough
items.current:
The short version of why this isn't an IntersectionObserver, plus what happens on each frame.

Visibility gate. Each watched element is tracked by an IntersectionObserver, so only on-screen elements are ever measured. A second observer tracks trigger zones with a root margin, so only zones near the viewport are considered.

One rAF loop. Scroll, resize, DOM mutation, ResizeObserver and observer callbacks all funnel into one coalesced requestAnimationFrame. Overlap and viewport registrations share that loop.

Read, commit, then notify. Per frame, every unique element rect is read once. Classes, ownership and observer targets are committed before consumer callbacks, so reentrant teardown cannot resurrect stale work.

Minimal class churn. A class is added or removed only when the winning zone actually changes, so scrolling within one zone writes to the DOM zero times. Rects are still read each frame.

Idle pages skip the measuring. With no visible overlap work and no viewport registrations, a scroll frame returns before scheduling anything. The passive scroll and resize listeners stay attached — they are what notices the page becoming busy again.

items.title: Overriding a composed token
items.current: If the property you're changing is a variable that itself references another one — a shadow composite, a gradient, a border shorthand — declared on :root, then overriding the inner variable from an over-* class does nothing. CSS bakes the nested var() once, where the composite is declared, and the result inherits down. Re-declare the composite on the watched element so it re-bakes against that element's value.

Overriding the inner variable from an over-* class does nothing. CSS bakes the nested var() once, where the composite is declared, and the result inherits down. Re-declare the composite on the watched element so it re-bakes against that element's value.
items.reason: This was the hardest sentence on the page to read: a conditional with a dashed list dropped into the middle of it, so "declared on :root" arrived seven words after the noun it modifies. Setting up the situation first, then stating what happens, costs one extra sentence and makes it followable.
items.note: Biggest structural change in this round. The three technical sentences after it are untouched.

items.title: Sticky overflow and stacking
items.current:
position: sticky and overflow

A sticky watched element won't stick if an ancestor has overflow: hidden, auto, or scroll. Put clipping on a sibling layer, not an ancestor of the sticky element.

Stacking is not considered

Overlap ignores z-index. At one nesting depth the larger physical coverage wins, which may not be the element actually painted on top.
items.proposed:

Stacking is not considered

items.reason: Two short entries, no dashes, and each names a limit plus the workaround where one exists. No workaround is invented for z-index, because there isn't one.

items.title: Neither is clipping
items.current: getBoundingClientRect reports where an element would be, not what's visible. A trigger zone inside a scrolling container still reports a full-size rect once it has scrolled out of view, so a watched element outside that container can pick up a zone nobody can see. When your zones live in a scroller, put the trigger class on the scroller itself — its rect is the visible box — and relabel it from script as its content scrolls.

items.reason: Paired dashes become a relative clause. The fix sentence now reads as one instruction rather than an instruction with an interruption wedged into it.
items.body: Earlier this round the entry gained "outside that container" and "from script", both of which were needed, since the old wording implied any watched element was at risk and made the relabelling sound automatic. It also dropped "The playground on this page does exactly that", which stopped being true once the playground moved to per-column proxy strips.

items.title: One element gets one answer
items.current: Majority overlap resolves per watched element, so a wide element spanning two zones takes a single class — and half of it ends up styled for the wrong background. A bar across the full content width hits this constantly. The fix is not in the library: watch the regions instead of the container. Wrap each cluster of content in its own watched element and each resolves its own zone, in the same frame, from the same watcher. The header on this page does exactly that — its left and right ends carry different classes whenever they sit over different zones. Nesting is safe because a watched element only ever resolves against elements carrying a trigger class, so the container it sits inside is invisible to it.

items.title: refresh(), schedule() and vertical-only viewport state
items.current:
Dynamic triggers need refresh()

Trigger zones are indexed on refresh() — at adapter mount, or via refreshCanvasWatch() — not continuously observed for class changes. Adding a zone, or changing an existing zone's trigger class, needs a re-scan.

Unobservable motion needs schedule()

Scroll, resize, relevant DOM mutations, target resizing and viewport-boundary crossings invalidate geometry. Call schedule() after motion that changes geometry without producing one of those signals.

Viewport state is vertical only

observeViewport and canvasWatch classify a reference against the viewport's top and bottom edges. Horizontal position is deliberately ignored, so an element parked far off to the side still reports within.

items.body: The vertical-only entry is new this round. It says the behaviour is deliberate and then gives the surprising case plainly, rather than leaving you to find it.

items.title: Purely presentational
items.current: canvas-watch is purely presentational. It adds and removes one class. It sets no ARIA attributes, announces nothing to assistive technology, and never alters content or focus order. Whether it changes layout is entirely down to what your over-* rules declare.
items.proposed: canvas-watch is purely presentational. It adds and removes one class. It sets no ARIA attributes, announces nothing to assistive technology, and never alters content or focus order. Whether it changes layout is entirely down to what your over-* rules declare.
items.reason: Four sentences, no dashes. It says what the library doesn't do, specifically, then hands back the one thing it can't control.

items.title: Contrast warning
items.current: Contrast is your responsibility, and it matters more the more you restyle. A shadow that misses 3:1 is cosmetic; text that lands at 2:1 because the panel behind it changed is a WCAG 1.4.3 failure. If your over-* rules touch text, border, or icon colour, check every zone — the library only tells you which one you're over, it has no idea whether the result is legible.

items.reason: The semicolon was a "but", and that contrast is the entire point of the sentence, so it should be a word. The dash becomes a full stop and the comma splice after it goes, which leaves the last line landing on its own.
items.note: The 3:1, 2:1 and 1.4.3 references are untouched. They're what make the warning actionable.

items.title: Reduced motion and browser support
items.current:
Reduced motion is the consumer's call. Put any transition on the properties you change behind @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce).

Under the hood it needs IntersectionObserver, ResizeObserver, MutationObserver, requestAnimationFrame and CustomEvent. The test suite runs in headless Chromium; other engines are not covered by CI. It is SSR-safe: createCanvasWatcher returns a no-op when window and document are absent, and the Svelte adapter only runs on the client.

items.note: "Other engines aren't covered by CI" is the sentence most libraries leave out, and stating the tested engine instead of claiming broad support is the accurate version. Worth keeping even though it reads as a negative.
